label: Lie Groups
notes: This chapter, printed pages 150 through 173, opens the door to Lie theory. A Lie group fuses two grammars: a smooth manifold and a group whose multiplication and inversion are smooth maps. Stress that the entire chapter is powered by one consequence, namely that translation by a fixed element is a diffeomorphism.

label: Definition of a Lie Group
notes: Define a Lie group as a smooth manifold carrying a group structure whose multiplication and inversion are smooth. Point out that smoothness of inversion is sometimes automatic, but here we just demand it. Emphasize the boundaryless requirement and remind students that the group identity sits at a distinguished point of the manifold.

label: Examples of Lie Groups
notes: Walk through the standard catalogue: the additive vector space, the general linear group as an open subset of matrix space, the special linear, orthogonal, special orthogonal, unitary groups, the circle, and tori as quotients. Highlight that determinant and transpose conditions cut these groups out as level sets or open sets.

label: Left Translation
notes: Introduce left translation as multiplication on the left by a fixed element. Show that it is a diffeomorphism with smooth inverse given by the opposite element. This is the workhorse of the chapter: it carries the identity to any chosen group element and lets local data at the identity propagate across the whole manifold.

label: Left-Invariant Vector Fields
notes: A vector field is left-invariant when every left translation pushes it forward to itself. Explain that such a field is completely determined by its single value at the identity, because translation carries that one tangent vector to every other point. This rigid correspondence is the bridge to the Lie algebra constructed next.

label: The Lie Algebra
notes: Define the Lie algebra as the space of left-invariant vector fields, closed under the Lie bracket. Stress the evaluation isomorphism with the tangent space at the identity, so the Lie algebra has the same dimension as the group. The bracket on identity vectors is inherited by transporting fields and bracketing them.

label: One-Parameter Subgroups
notes: A one-parameter subgroup is a smooth homomorphism from the real line into the group. Explain that each one is the integral curve through the identity of a left-invariant field, and conversely every left-invariant field generates one. This is the seed of the exponential map developed in later chapters.

label: Homomorphisms and Covering
notes: A Lie group homomorphism is a smooth group homomorphism; isomorphisms are smooth bijections with smooth inverse. Use the exponential wrapping of the line onto the circle as the model: it respects multiplication, has the integers as kernel, and locally looks like a diffeomorphism while globally covering the circle infinitely.

label: Lie Subgroups
notes: Distinguish embedded from immersed Lie subgroups. Kernels of homomorphisms are properly embedded, hence closed. The cautionary example is the irrational line on the torus: an injective homomorphism whose image is immersed but dense, so not embedded. Closedness and embeddedness coincide for Lie subgroups, which is far stronger than for general submanifolds.

label: Group Actions
notes: A smooth action assigns to each group element a diffeomorphism of a manifold, compatibly with multiplication. The orbit is the image of the orbit map and the stabilizer is its fiber. For the rotation action on the plane, nonzero points trace circles with trivial stabilizer while the origin is fixed by the whole group.

label: Equivariance and Constant Rank
notes: An equivariant map intertwines two actions. When the domain action is transitive, the group moves any tangent calculation to any other point, so the differential has the same rank everywhere. Present the tangent square: vertical arrows are linear isomorphisms induced by translations, forcing the two horizontal maps to share a rank.

label: The Circle and the Torus
notes: Treat the circle as the cleanest compact abelian Lie group, with multiplication being angle addition and translations being rigid rotations. The torus is its higher-dimensional analogue, a product of circles covered by Euclidean space. These translations are exactly the flows of the constant left-invariant fields on the group.

label: Synthesis
notes: Close by tying the threads together: translations turn identity data into global structure, the Lie algebra captures the group near the identity, homomorphisms have constant rank, subgroups are rigid, and actions realize groups as families of diffeomorphisms. Preview that the Lie algebra and exponential map will dominate the chapters ahead.
